en: The Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. This...

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra requested the bhikṣus to listen to his discourse on the Dharma, which was excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its conclusion; it was well-expounded, clearly analyzed, and possessed of complete purity. "Listen to the conduct of the Venerable One, who is named 'Endowed with the Practice of Dharma' (Dharmapratipanna)"; you should listen with a virtuous mind and attend to it with careful mindfulness.
"Monks, you should act as the Venerable has spoken and listen to the Venerable Śāriputra.
The Venerable Śāriputra will then explain the twelve-fold assembly that can lead one to the path of the noble ones."

“What are the twelve? First, being able to instruct oneself; second, being able to instruct others as well; third, following among ordinary people; fourth, following among the wise; fifth, possessing the complete faculties; sixth, not following worldly occupations; seventh, rejoicing in the sight of the wise; eighth, the Buddha’s presence; ninth, the teaching of the Dharma; tenth, being able to receive the Dharma once it has been taught; eleventh, being able to listen to and accept external teachings; twelfth, being able to practice according to what has been attained.”
This constitutes the twelve assemblies of the worthy.
To attain the Way of the worthy, one should practice according to this.
"If one intends to speak of other persons in a sutra, it should be explained by means of these twenty chapters."

What are the twenty? First, speaking well; second, speaking much; third, speaking coherently from beginning to end; fourth, speaking in proper sequence; fifth, speaking with joy; sixth, speaking what is appropriate; seventh, speaking to clarify the meaning; eighth, speaking to remove shame; ninth, speaking so as not to commit a great error; tenth, speaking to discipline; eleventh, speaking appropriately; twelfth, speaking without distraction; thirteenth, speaking according to the Dharma; fourteenth, speaking in accordance with the assembly; fifteenth, speaking with an even mind; sixteenth, speaking to assist and protect the mind; seventeenth, not speaking for the sake of seeking fame; eighteenth, not speaking for the sake of profit; nineteenth, not speaking out of self-display; twentieth, not speaking to discipline others.
"If a wise bhikṣu wishes to preach for others, he should preach these twenty items.
Śāriputra further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who wish to hear the Dharma should possess sixteen practices."

What are these sixteen? First, one should listen at a time when it is possible to hear; second, one should be extensively learned; third, one should listen with an attentive ear; fourth, one should attend to the matter; fifth, one should not criticize superficially; sixth, one should not speak of faults; seventh, one should not seek out long and short [faults]; eighth, one should respect the Dharma; ninth, one should respect the teacher of the Dharma; tenth, one should not treat the Dharma lightly; eleventh, one should likewise not treat the teacher of the Dharma lightly; twelfth, one should likewise not treat oneself lightly; thirteenth, one should maintain a single-minded focus; fourteenth, one should have no other thoughts; fifteenth, one should correctly uphold the mind; sixteenth, one should clearly comprehend all thoughts so that the hearing of the Dharma is correct.
“If a wise person wishes to hear the Dharma, they should listen to it by means of these sixteen modes.
What are the sixteen?

First, hearing the Dharma from time to time; second, hearing much of the Dharma; third, hearing the Dharma with attentive ears; fourth, hearing the Dharma regarding its actual substance; fifth, hearing the Dharma without reproaching it; sixth, hearing the Dharma without seeking faults; seventh, hearing the Dharma with reverence for the Dharma; eighth, hearing the Dharma with reverence for the expounder of the sutras; ninth, hearing the Dharma without treating the Dharma lightly; tenth, hearing the Dharma without treating the expounder of the Dharma lightly; eleventh, hearing the Dharma without treating oneself lightly; twelfth, hearing the Dharma with a single-minded focus; thirteenth, hearing the Dharma without having ulterior motives; fourteenth, hearing the Dharma with a mind set uprightly; fifteenth, hearing the Dharma with all one’s attention focused on a single purpose; sixteenth, hearing the Dharma with a concentrated and settled mind.
"If a wise person wishes to hear the Dharma, they should do so by following these sixteen analogies for hearing the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma as described above, they will give rise to faith and mental satisfaction; from this, they shall reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
Having heard such a Dharma, one gives rise to the noble love that is free from desire; from this, one ultimately attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having heard such a Dharma, one gives rise to a joyful mind of love; from this, one attains the unconditioned.
Having heard such a Dharma, one abandons the mind of attachment to evil and attains a concentrated mind; from this, one reaches the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having heard such a Dharma, one attains the relinquishing of doubt and views, becoming further enlightened, and is most excellently led toward the unconditioned.

Having heard such a Dharma as this, one then perceives that the aggregates (skandhas) are non-existent; one then perceives the aggregates as empty; one then perceives the aggregates as light. Through these perceptions, the mind becomes liberated, the mind becomes pure, the mind becomes stilled, and the mind attains liberation; in this way, one proceeds from this toward the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

Having heard the Dharma in this way, one perceives that all worldly activities and views are empty; no longer proceeding toward or dwelling therein, craving is exhausted, abandoned, and extinguished. Thus, the mind turns toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the mind comes to rest, and liberation is attained; it is by means of this that one reaches the unconditioned.
Having heard the Dharma in this way, one intends to practice accordingly; by practicing alone and severing delusions, one attains the first vow and thereby reaches the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having heard such a Dharma, one acts for the sake of purifying the eye that sees the Four Truths, and thereby reaches the unconditioned.
Having heard such a Dharma as this, one fulfills their practice and thereby attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Having heard such a Dharma as this, the noble disciple who does not trouble the speaker also gains happiness from hearing it, does not violate the teaching, and follows after peace; thus, the fulfillment of what they seek is achieved through these ten factors that lead to wise conduct.

What are the ten? First, a virtuous friend; second, virtuous precepts; third, virtuous fellow students; fourth, knowing the intention of receiving [the teaching]; fifth, receiving instruction; sixth, questioning; seventh, hearing the sūtras; eighth, discussing the sūtras in assembly; ninth, experiencing fear due to causes and conditions for fear; tenth, when one feels shame regarding fear, observing its original source at that very moment.

One then cuts off all unwholesome dharmas; being able to cut them off by observing from the root and thereby rejecting these dharmas, one attains concentration of mind and mastery, all because of observing from the root. Thus, having truly observed from the root, the disciple of the Way has abandoned [them].
"One may then practice ten contemplations. What are these ten? First, the contemplation of impurity;

second, the contemplation of impermanence; third, the contemplation of suffering as arising from impermanence; fourth, the contemplation of non-self as arising from suffering; fifth, the contemplation of the foulness of food; sixth, the contemplation of detachment from all worldly pleasures; seventh, the contemplation of mindfulness of death; eighth, the contemplation of ignorance; ninth, the contemplation of the withdrawal of the mind; and tenth, the contemplation of cessation."
“Venerable sir, one who contemplates the thought of impurity follows fourteen wrong states.
What are these fourteen?

First, living together with one’s own kin while losing one’s composure; second, seeing greed within one’s own kin; third, being impulsive in desire; fourth, having impure thoughts and not knowing the practice of the Dharma; fifth, being unable to contemplate impurity; sixth, associating with those who perform evil deeds; seventh, not recognizing what is right; eighth, not serving [the teacher]; ninth, not inquiring [about the Dharma]; tenth, not guarding the sense faculties; eleventh, not knowing moderation in eating; twelfth, not practicing the yoga of the first and last watches of the night; thirteenth, being unable to sit alone in contemplation; and fourteenth, being unable to contemplate the thought of impermanence as it truly is.
“Wise one! One who conforms to the worldly desire for the contemplation of impermanence and suffering conforms to six unwholesome states.
What are these six?

First is insufficiency; second is lack of diligence; third is lack of faith; fourth is desire; fifth is not wishing to sit in secluded places; sixth is failing to attain the contemplation that views suffering as not-self.
The contemplation on the impurity of the body is for the purpose of not being attached to the craving for flavors;
the contemplation on the lack of delight in all things under heaven is because one understands that the worldly myriad phenomena cannot be pursued through greed;
the contemplation on death is for the purpose of practicing the clear contemplation that follows the departure of life.
"O Wise One! There are eleven deviations to which one may succumb.

What are these eleven? First is doubt; second is lack of mindfulness; third is physical restlessness; fourth is drowsiness; fifth is excessive exertion; sixth is laxity of exertion; seventh is false joy; eighth is fear; ninth is manifold discursive thought; tenth is lack of discernment; and eleventh is the contemplation of forms."

Furthermore, friend, for one who reflects, reflection leads to being separated from the Path; for one who has ceased reflection, if the mind is fixed on the Dharma, it leads to being separated from the Path. In this regard, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: [the desire for] sensual pleasure, [the desire for] existence, and [the desire for] non-existence. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the desire for sensual pleasure, the desire for existence, and the desire for non-existence. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: ignorance, lack of shame, and lack of dread. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon ignorance, lack of shame, and lack of dread. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: wrong view, wrong resolve, and wrong effort. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon wrong view, wrong resolve, and wrong effort. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong knowledge. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong knowledge. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: wrong liberation, wrong knowledge, and wrong vision. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon wrong liberation, wrong knowledge, and wrong vision. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: conceit, agitation, and ignorance. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon conceit, agitation, and ignorance. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward sensual desire, the underlying tendency toward aversion, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward sensual desire, the underlying tendency toward aversion, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward views, the underlying tendency toward doubt, and the underlying tendency toward adherence to rules and rituals. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward views, the underlying tendency toward doubt, and the underlying tendency toward adherence to rules and rituals. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward greed, the underlying tendency toward hatred, and the underlying tendency toward delusion. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward greed, the underlying tendency toward hatred, and the underlying tendency toward delusion. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward lust, the underlying tendency toward anger, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward lust, the underlying tendency toward anger, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward craving for form, the underlying tendency toward craving for the formless, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward craving for form, the underlying tendency toward craving for the formless, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward conceit, the underlying tendency toward restlessness, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward conceit, the underlying tendency toward restlessness, and the underlying tendency toward ignorance. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward self-identity, the underlying tendency toward doubt, and the underlying tendency toward attachment to rules and rituals. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward self-identity, the underlying tendency toward doubt, and the underlying tendency toward attachment to rules and rituals. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward sensual desire, the underlying tendency toward ill will, and the underlying tendency toward cruelty. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward sensual desire, the underlying tendency toward ill will, and the underlying tendency toward cruelty. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward gain, the underlying tendency toward fame, and the underlying tendency toward praise. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward gain, the underlying tendency toward fame, and the underlying tendency toward praise. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward birth, the underlying tendency toward old age, and the underlying tendency toward death. These three things cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. Therefore, friend, you should train yourself thus: "I shall abandon the underlying tendency toward birth, the underlying tendency toward old age, and the underlying tendency toward death. Thus should you train yourself. Furthermore, friend, there are three things that cause one to be separated from the Path, which, though not yet destroyed, must be destroyed. What are these three? They are: the underlying tendency toward sorrow, the underlying tendency toward lamentation, and the
What are the three?
First, desire; second, abandonment; third, sitting and walking.
"The perception of impurity, worthy one!"
There are fourteen practices that should be cultivated extensively. What are these fourteen? First, not dwelling together with the group of householders;

second, the restraint of the mind; third, not seeing the group of householders; fourth, self-guarding; fifth, having no haste or desire; sixth, purifying one's thoughts so as not to follow after them; seventh, purifying one's thoughts so as not to dwell upon them; eighth, not desiring to associate with those who practice worldly ways; ninth, not desiring to accept worldly practices; tenth, guarding the sense faculties; eleventh, moderation in eating; twelfth, practicing vigilance during the first and last watches of the night without sleeping; thirteenth, cultivating weariness toward desires and sitting alone; and fourteenth, frequently cultivating the contemplation of impurity as it truly is.
"O Wise One!
From this practice one cuts off craving and desire.
By frequently cultivating the perception of impermanence, one cuts off craving and desire from this."
Having practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the perception of extreme suffering, one thereby severs delusion;
having practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the perception that suffering is not the self, one thereby severs the view of a self;
having practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the perception of the loathsomeness of food, one thereby severs craving.
When one has practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the perception of the world as unattractive, one thereby severs attachment to the world;
when one has practiced, cultivated, and frequently attended to the perception of death, one thereby severs attachment to life;
when one has practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed the perception of light, one thereby attains clear vision.
Furthermore, by cultivating, practicing, and frequently performing the perception of repulsiveness, one abandons craving;
by cultivating, practicing, and frequently performing the perception of cessation, one attains liberation from the false.
Thus, O worthy one, the disciple of the noble one should truly receive [the teaching].
"O worthy one! [he said].
There are twenty qualities of a disciple of the Way that prevent them from following the Way.
What are these twenty?

First, dwelling together without practicing the Path; second, not inquiring [into the Dharma]; third, practicing without knowing what is appropriate; fourth, being dull-witted; fifth, engaging in evil conduct; sixth, having a covetous mind; seventh, being preoccupied with many affairs; eighth, lacking diligence; ninth, destroying one's own refuge through mutual [corruption]; tenth, [attachment to] physical form; eleventh, seeking self-aggrandizement; twelfth, being inverted; thirteenth, losing the right intention; fourteenth, greed; fifteen, dwelling together with an unwholesome group; sixteen, failing to guard the gates of the senses; seventeen, not knowing moderation in eating; eighteen, failing to practice during the first and last watches of the night; nineteen, taking no delight in solitary sitting and reflection; twentieth, failing to contemplate things as they truly are.
"Venerable one! These twenty matters cause one to stray from the Path.
For one who has not yet abandoned what should be abandoned, there are eleven things that are most prevalent. What are these eleven?"

First is for the sake of desire; second, for the sake of attainment; third, for the sake of convenience of view; fourth, for the sake of having support; fifth, for the sake of avoiding waste; sixth, for the sake of victory; seventh, for the sake of attaining the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); eighth, for the sake of compliance; ninth, for the sake of inquiry; tenth, for the sake of solitary self-guarding; eleventh, for the sake of contemplation according to reality.
Thus it has been correctly joined.
"Worthy one!
A disciple of the noble path possesses many twenty qualities."

What are these twenty? First, dwelling together with those who practice the Path; second, inquiry; third, knowing what should be done regarding one's conduct; fourth, not being dull-witted; fifth, mutual practice; sixth, not being mired in greed; seventh, having few affairs; eighth, not abandoning diligence; ninth, being free from calamities; tenth, not conforming to external appearances; eleventh, not seeking self-aggrandizement; twelfth, being without inversion; thirteenth, guarding the mind; fourteenth, not being covetous; fifteenth, dwelling in harmony with the virtuous community; sixteenth, guarding the gates of the sense faculties; seventeenth, knowing moderation in eating; eighteenth, being able to practice during the first and last watches of the night; nineteenth, delighting in solitary reflection; twentieth, practicing according to reality.
“If it is so, worthy one!
There are twenty-two further points regarding the practice of the path by one who has already become a śramaṇa, which should be contemplated as being urgent.

What are the twenty-two? First, that one has already accepted an unattractive state; second, that one has already engaged in various karmic actions; third, that my life depends upon others; fourth, that until the end of my life I must seek clothing, food, medicine for sickness and emaciation, and bedding; fifth, that until the end of my life my desires will remain covered; sixth, that until the end of my life there are human desires for pleasure, yet having become a śramaṇa, I observe these with haste;

seventh, so that my body may not be harmed or destroyed; eighth, so that I may attain solitary joy in the midst of emptiness; ninth, so that I do not follow after sinful gains when receiving food; tenth, so that my body does not lose its precepts; eleventh, so that I do not engage in debate with those who are clever and of the same path regarding me.

12. May I, while practicing my path in accordance with the four virtues within the prescribed curriculum, be able to speak when questioned by fellow practitioners at the time my life comes to an end; let not one who wishes to practice the Path for even a moment fail to contemplate this.

13. May I be able to contemplate that the aggregates (*skandha*) are impermanent. 14. May I be able to contemplate that the aggregates are non-existent. 15. May I be able to contemplate that the aggregates are not substantial, so that my mind may turn away from them and rely upon liberation; let the practitioner of the Path urgently contemplate this. 16.

May I contemplate the world as empty, unattached, the exhaustion of craving, detachment, cessation, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); may my mind observe this, may pleasant feelings cease, and may I attain liberation. When one is free from the afflictions of form, time, and place, one should thus contemplate.

Seventeenth is birth: one has not yet attained deliverance from birth. Eighteenth is old age: one has not yet attained deliverance from old age. Nineteenth is illness: one has not yet attained deliverance from illness. Twentieth is the law of death: one has not yet attained deliverance from the law of death; having avoided the physical form, one must urgently contemplate this.

Twenty-first is that all things I love must eventually part—whether through loss, being taken away by others, or death—they cannot remain long; having avoided the physical form, one must urgently contemplate the distinctions of time and place.

Twenty-second is that each person attains results according to their own conduct, each has their own conduct as their root, each undergoes suffering according to their own conduct, and each receives the fruits of their own good and evil deeds; having avoided the physical form, one must urgently contemplate the distinctions of time and place.
"By means of these twenty-two practices, having trained in them, practiced them, and cultivated them extensively, one fulfills the state of a śramaṇa; this is also what the practitioner contemplates.
Having fulfilled what is contemplated by the practitioner of a śramaṇa, one is then able to fulfill the seven contemplations."

What are the seven? First, entering by practicing constantly without ceasing; second, not turning back; third, not contending; fourth, upright mindfulness; fifth, not giving rise to a mind of arrogance; sixth, seeking only food and clothing while remaining in the world; and seventh, attaining mastery through the cessation of mental activity.
Thus it is, worthy one!

For countless days and nights, the mental consciousness has been directed toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; because it could not be restrained while remaining in the world, once it is able to exercise restraint and attain stillness, it enters the seed of the Deathless.
“O worthy one, these twenty types of conduct must be undertaken;
for one who has not yet attained the Path, they should be a cause for apprehension. What are these twenty?
First, there is no entry into emptiness; second, one does not learn how to die; third, one casts oneself onto a shore;
fourth, one believes in and fears the wrong direction; fifth, one does not know and does not fear the right direction;
sixth, one does not know the Path; seventh, one does not attain meditative concentration; eighth, there is suffering in future lives; ninth, it is difficult for the wise to meet; tenth—
1. To open the gate of the world for those who are no different from worldly people; 2. To build a bridge for those who have not yet done so, enabling them to avoid the hells;
3. To liberate those who have not yet understood the evil realms; 4. For the sake of those who are universally suspicious and beyond counting; 5.
To provide the essential means for the world for those who have not yet attained it; 6. To prevent death during times of dullness and folly.
Sixteenth, because one cannot be "A" while performing the deeds of "B," one should not act; seventeenth, that which is not to be done should likewise not be done;
eighteenth, in non-action there is neither fortune nor misfortune; nineteenth, that which has already been done must not be forgotten;
twentieth, there is only the existence of one's own action, only the following of one's own action, and only the original nature of one's own action.
It is simply that one returns to oneself.
If all good and evil exists within oneself, one should merely accept and practice it; as for the world of vessels and its inhabitants, one should regard them with a sense of awe.

"By means of these twenty causes and conditions, the mind that was evil becomes further evil, fear becomes further fear, and aversion becomes further aversion; thus, there are twenty ways in which the movement of the mind is swiftly stilled."
What are the twenty?
First, through mindfulness of the mind, the mind quickly comes to rest; second, through knowing the mind within the mind, the mind quickly comes to rest;

third, through the mind being already one-pointed, the mind quickly comes to rest; fourth, through right mindfulness, knowing the mind, the mind quickly comes to rest; fifth, through right... [text continues]

1. Stopping through the application of mindfulness; 2. Stopping through the application of mindfulness arising from correctness; 3. Stopping through the application of mindfulness by means of gathering;
4. Stopping through the application of mindfulness by means of assistance; 5. Stopping through the application of mindfulness by means of guarding; 6.
Stopping through the application of mindfulness by practicing the four foundations of mindfulness; 7. Stopping through the application of mindfulness by means of the four right efforts.
Twelfth is the rapid stilling of the mind through the four bases of psychic power; thirteenth is the rapid stilling of the mind by avoiding what is improper to practice;

fourteenth is the rapid stilling of the mind by approaching the proper sphere of conduct; fifteenth is the rapid stilling of the mind by having that which is to be relied upon and followed in training;
sixteenth is the rapid stilling of the mind by both reciting and understanding [the teachings]; seventeenth is...
17. One should quickly still the mind that is full of sorrow; 18. one should quickly still the mind that is full of much worldly delight;
19. one should quickly still the mind that is preoccupied with objects of perception; 20. one should quickly still the mind that is engaged in such [worldly] conduct.
Thus it is, worthy one!
A disciple of the Way should know that there are eleven untimely deaths.
What are these eleven?

First, frequenting social gatherings; second, eating excessively; third, engaging in many affairs; fourth, talking too much; fifth, excessive sleepiness; sixth, delighting in traveling in groups; seventh, enjoying living together with others; eighth, indulging in physical pleasures; ninth, being frivolous; tenth, being lustful; eleventh, residing in unwholesome districts and counties.
Dwelling in this, O worthy one!
Whatever transgressions have not yet been severed, you should sever them.
Furthermore, you should train in the ten mutual [practices].

What are the ten? First is the mutual [practice] of concentration of mind; second is the mutual [practice] of concentration of cessation; third is the mutual [practice] of concentration of arising; fourth is the mutual [practice] of cessation; fifth is the mutual [practice] of restraint; sixth is the mutual [practice] of protection; seventh is the mutual [practice] of the foundation; eighth is the mutual [practice] of protection against transgression; ninth is the mutual [practice] of skillful means; tenth is the mutual [practice] of entry.

Regarding those who thus enter into mutual [practice], the disciples on the path possess thirteen virtues. What are these thirteen? First, by recollecting the Tathāgata, they immediately attain joyful faith, and thus joy arises.

Second, it is the same regarding the Dharma. Third, it is the same regarding the learners (*śaikṣa*). Fourth, it is the same regarding one's own observance of the precepts. Fifth, it is the same regarding the observance of the precepts by others. Sixth, it is the same regarding one’s own attainment [of merit]. Seventh, it is the same regarding the attainment [of merit] by others. Eighth, it is the same regarding one’s own giving. Ninth, it is the same regarding the giving of others. Tenth, the Path extensively removes suffering. Eleventh, the world extensively expounds the sūtras so that they may be contemplated. Twelfth, one turns back from countless practices of evil. Thirteenth, one enters into the arising of joy through countless practices of wholesome dharmas; having attained faith, one is able to possess the seeds of joy.
Regarding this joy, a disciple of the Path should practice by relying on four things so as to bring five qualities to fulfillment.
What are the four things to rely upon?
First, reliance on the Dharma; second, reliance on desire; third, reliance on further exertion; and fourth, reliance on solitary sitting, free from other attachments.
“What are the five dharmas that, when fulfilled, serve as the requisites for the Path?
First is joy; second is affection; third is reliance; fourth is happiness; and fifth is concentration.”
“For one who practices such joy, the disciple on the path is able to attain the cessation of eight wounds.
What are these eight? First is the wound of desire;

second is the wound of hatred; third is the wound of delusion; fourth is the wound of pride; fifth is the wound of craving; sixth is the wound of ignorance; seventh is the wound of gain, honor, and fame; and eighth is the wound of doubt that remains unresolved.”
The practitioner having already accomplished this, being able to submerge and extinguish the eight wounds, shall then have attained transcendence of the world.
"One does not study ten things. What are these ten?"

First is right view through learning; second is right resolve; third is right speech; fourth is right action; fifth is right livelihood; sixth is right effort; seventh is right mindfulness; eighth is right concentration; ninth is right liberation; and tenth is right knowledge.

By means of these ten things not to be learned, through these causes and conditions, one encounters the direct path; thereupon, one abandons the five kinds of directness, follows the six kinds of [right] conduct, and maintains the four bases of tranquility (*śamatha*). Having not failed to realize the truths, one has abandoned distress; being unattached to seeking, one attains cessation. With the cessation of bodily activity, the cessation of vocal activity, and the cessation of mental activity, the mind’s deliberations are transcended. Being most wise and having transcended all without remainder, one who has thus fulfilled their practice is called "Supreme" (*uttama*).
"O Wise One!

This which is called 'the wise one,' the subsequent mind and consciousness, having come from afar, does not act, does not accumulate, and does not reassemble; it simply ceases. This is the essential cutting off of suffering."

"What has been taught above, O worthy one, is the Dharma-discourse that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is beneficial and relevant, perfectly pure and a pure exposition of the essential path. This is what is called the causal condition for the Dharma that possesses benefit."
"That which was stated at the beginning was for this reason stated.
Thus spoke the Venerable Śāriputra.
The bhikṣus received it with a sincere mind and thus bore in mind what was said.
The Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma Spoken by the Buddha.
